item.title: The Fast of The 17th of Tammuz
item.description:
What is the purpose of the 17th of Tammuz fast? Zekhariah names four fasts, in Tishrei, Tevet, Av and Tammuz. They were instituted by the prophets, and the point is not the fast itself but reflection, teshuvah and the hope of the Temple's rebuilding.

item.title: Exemptions from the Fast of the 17th of Tammuz
item.description:
Who must fast on the 17th of Tammuz? Men and women equally, not children. A pregnant or nursing woman, a woman within two years of birth according to Hakham Ovadia, the ill and the very elderly are exempt. Only eating and drinking are restricted; haircuts and showers are permitted.

item.title: What's Not Allowed during the Three Weeks
item.description:
The Three Weeks do not appear in the Gemara, whose restrictions begin only on Rosh Hodesh Av. The Midrash on Eikhah, Ben HaMesarim, gives this period its name. The Rabbi covers the two points in the Shulhan Arukh: weddings and reciting Shehiyanu on new clothes, and Shabbat.

item.title: The Origins of the Three Weeks
item.description:
Where does the idea of the Three Weeks come from? It is absent from the Talmud and the Rambam. It derives from a Midrash on Eikhah about being caught between the straits, and is first named by Rav Hai Gaon, so the restrictions are later customs rather than Talmudic law.

item.title: The Haftarot of the Three Weeks
item.description:
Why are there three Haftarot of rebuke between the seventeenth of Tammuz and Tisha BeAv? They come from the first two chapters of Yirmiyahu and the first of Yeshayahu. The shiur reviews Yirmiyahu's almond blossom and boiling pot, and the custom's source in Pesikta, between the fifth and seventh centuries.

item.title: Are There Any Restrictions during the Three Weeks
item.description:
What does the Shulhan Arukh actually restrict during the Three Weeks? Only four things are recorded: fasting each day from the seventeenth of Tammuz, which few do, avoiding meat or wine, avoiding dangerous activity, and a recommendation not to say Shehiyanu. Beyond that, for Sephardim and from the Gemara for Ashkenazim, the rest is custom.

item.title: Guidelines to the Nine Days
item.description:
How should we lower joy during the nine days? The Mishnah says we reduce simhah in Av. Tosafot, the Mishnah Berurah and Magen Avraham take this to mean no joy at all, while the Rambam reads it as reducing. The shiur covers entertainment, weddings, building and non-essential purchases, with haircuts left for later.

item.title: The Nine Days
item.description:
What changes from Rosh Hodesh Av until Tisha BeAv? The Mishnah says we reduce joy. Tosafot read this as no joy at all, as the Mishnah Berurah and Magen Avraham codify, while the Rambam takes it literally. Marriages, non-essential building and luxury transactions are to be avoided, and haircuts are deferred.

item.title: Tisha BeAv: Its Status in Relation to Other Fasts
item.description:
How does Tisha BeAv differ from other fasts and from Yom Kippur? It is a full 24 hours, pregnant and nursing women must begin fasting, and any ill person may eat, unlike Yom Kippur. It adds bans on greeting and Torah study, and a woman who gave birth is exempt for 30 days.

item.title: Seating Arrangements on Tisha BeAv: Tisha BeAv Customs Part 2
item.description:

item.title: What Is Not Allowed During the Nine Days
item.description:
How much simhah is allowed in the Nine Days? The Mishnah says we reduce it, which Tosafot, the Mishnah Berurah and the Magen Avraham take as refraining from joyful things, while the Rambam reads it more literally. item.title: The Restrictions of the Week of Tisha BeAv
item.description:
What changes in the week of Tisha BeAv itself? Beyond the Three Weeks and Nine Days restrictions, two rules apply only in that week: no haircuts or shaving, and no laundering or putting on freshly washed clothes. The shiur explains the lenient practice of wearing clothes briefly beforehand so they are no longer fresh.

item.title: A Thought for 17 Tammuz and 3 Weeks: Gadgets and Distractions
item.description:
What do the five tragedies of 17 Tammuz have in common? Four concern the Beit HaMikdash, and the fifth is Moshe breaking the tablets over the golden calf, made as an intermediary after they lost him. The thought for the Three Weeks: gadgets and amulets must not become distractions from a direct relationship with God.
